title: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
summary: Why zero-shot dense retrieval is hard, how HyDE turns a query into LLM-written fake answers, averages their embeddings and searches real documents, what it gains, what it costs and when it hurts.
outcomes: Explain why an unsupervised encoder ranks real answers better from a fake answer than from the raw query
Compute a HyDE query vector from N hypothetical document embeddings plus the query, and the ranking it produces
Estimate the latency and token cost of N generations, sequential or in parallel
Recognize when HyDE hurts: ambiguous or unfamiliar queries, shared hallucinations, strong retrievers
Compare HyDE with query2doc and pick where each fits in a production search stack

lessons.title: Why a raw query is a poor probe for an unsupervised encoder

blocks.md: From the prerequisite course: a dense retriever embeds the query and every document into vectors and returns the documents with the highest inner product (or cosine). That only works if the encoders were trained so that *query* vectors land near the vectors of *relevant documents*. Training that usually needs relevance labels: many (query, relevant passage) pairs, for example the MS MARCO collection.

Gao, Ma, Lin and Callan (2022) ask what to do when no such labels exist: a new product, a new language, a private corpus. They also note that MS MARCO restricts commercial use, so it cannot always be borrowed. Their goal is **fully zero-shot dense retrieval**: no relevance labels, no training on the target corpus, works out of the box.

blocks.caption: Equation 1 of the HyDE paper. The hard part is learning two encoders whose inner product means relevance, which needs relevance judgments to fit.

blocks.md: There is an encoder that needs no labels: **Contriever** (Izacard et al., 2021), trained with contrastive learning on unlabeled text. Contrastive pre-training teaches it *document-document* similarity: two pieces of text about the same thing get close vectors. A short question is not shaped like a document, so using Contriever directly for query-document matching is weak. On TREC DL19 (web passages) Contriever scores nDCG@10 44.5, below plain BM25 at 50.6.

Here is a toy that makes the shape problem concrete. Each text gets a 4-number embedding with readable dimensions: *dental*, *duration* (states how long something takes), *question phrasing*, and *removal / how-to*. The query is the paper's own demo query: `how long does it take to remove wisdom tooth`. The corpus has five passages; D1 (an extraction takes 20 to 40 minutes) is the one we want.

scenes.caption: Six toy vectors, each scaled to length about 1. Simplified: real Contriever vectors have 768 dimensions with no readable meaning; the 4 named axes here only make the geometry visible.
The query's largest value is on the question axis (0.74), because it is phrased as a question. Real answers like D1 and D2 have 0 there: answers do not ask things.
D3 is an FAQ title about tree stumps. It shares the question phrasing and the removal wording with the query, but nothing dental.

blocks.prompt: Score each document by inner product with the query vector. Which passage comes out on top: D1 (extraction time) or D3 (tree stump FAQ)?
blocks.reveal: D3 wins, 0.91 against 0.60 for D1. The query vector is dominated by *how it is phrased*, and the FAQ shares that phrasing. An encoder trained only on document-document similarity has no reason to discount question form, because it never saw labeled question-answer pairs.

blocks.title: Toy scores for the raw query (inner product)

scenes.caption: Query-only ranking: D3 0.91, D1 0.60, D2 0.55, D4 0.48, D5 0.48. The off-topic FAQ beats the real answer because it matches the question's form, not its content.

blocks.md: Short queries and long documents look different. A label-free encoder knows what *documents* resemble each other, but nobody taught it what *answers a question*. HyDE's trick is to stop comparing a question with answers at all.

blocks.question: Why does unsupervised Contriever score below BM25 on TREC DL19 (44.5 vs 50.6 nDCG@10), even though it is a neural model?
options: Its vectors have too few dimensions to separate passages
BM25 was tuned on the DL19 test queries
It learned document-document similarity without relevance labels, so query-to-document matching was never trained
Dense retrieval cannot work on web passages
blocks.explain: Contrastive pre-training on unlabeled text makes similar documents close, but nothing pushes a question toward its answers. Fine-tuned on MS MARCO, the same model (ContrieverFT) reaches 62.1, so capacity is not the problem.

blocks.question: A team has a new internal wiki, no click logs and no labeled queries. Which statement about their options is accurate?
options: A supervised dense retriever cannot be trained on in-domain labels yet, which is exactly the setting HyDE targets
They must label at least MS MARCO scale data before any dense retrieval works
BM25 is guaranteed to beat every dense method here
Contriever alone will match a fine-tuned retriever
blocks.explain: No relevance labels is the zero-shot setting of the HyDE paper. Contriever alone is usable but weak; BM25 is a strong baseline but not guaranteed best. The paper's answer is to move relevance modeling into a generative LLM.

lessons.title: The HyDE pipeline: generate, encode, average, search

blocks.md:
**HyDE** (Hypothetical Document Embeddings) splits retrieval into two tasks that need no relevance labels:

1. A *generative* task: an instruction-following LLM is asked to write a passage that answers the query. This is the **hypothetical document**. It is not real and may contain false details.
2. A *document-document similarity* task: the unsupervised contrastive encoder (Contriever) embeds the hypothetical document, and the search finds real corpus documents near that vector.

The paper's phrase for the second step is that the encoder's **dense bottleneck** acts as a lossy compressor: a 768-number vector cannot keep every invented name or number, so the hope is that it keeps the relevance pattern (topic, answer shape) and drops the made-up specifics. Retrieval is then *grounded*: the user gets real documents, never the generated text.

scenes.caption: The query is wrapped in an instruction such as Please write a passage to answer the question, and sent to the LLM.
The LLM samples N passages (temperature 0.7 in the paper). They read like answers, with possibly invented details.
The same Contriever that embedded the corpus embeds each hypothetical passage, and also the query itself.
The N+1 vectors are averaged into one query vector. No model is trained or fine-tuned anywhere in this pipeline.
A normal maximum inner product search over the existing index returns real documents. The index is the same one plain Contriever would use.

blocks.tex: \hat v_q = \frac{1}{N+1}\Big[\sum_{k=1}^{N} f(\hat d_k) + f(q)\Big], \qquad \hat d_k \sim g(q, \mathrm{INST})
blocks.caption: Equation 8 of the paper. f is the contrastive encoder, g the instruction-following LM, INST the instruction. Equation 7 is the same average without the f(q) term.

blocks.md: Why an average? The paper treats the hypothetical vector as a random variable and estimates its expectation $\mathbb{E}[f(g(q,\mathrm{INST}))]$ by sampling N documents. It assumes this distribution has a single mode, which means the query is not ambiguous; ambiguous queries are explicitly left to future work. Adding $f(q)$ treats the query itself as one more hypothesis.

The instruction changes per task, which is how HyDE adapts to new tasks with no training. From the paper's appendix and the released `promptor.py`:

- Web search: Please write a passage to answer the question
- SciFact: Please write a scientific paper passage to support/refute the claim
- ArguAna: Please write a counter argument for the passage
- FiQA: Please write a financial article passage to answer the question
- Mr.TyDi: Please write a passage in Swahili/Korean/Japanese/Bengali to answer the question in detail

blocks.title: The encode step from the official repo, on the toy
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

def encode(query, hypothesis_documents, encoder):
    all_emb_c = []
    for c in [query] + hypothesis_documents:
        c_emb = encoder.encode(c)
        all_emb_c.append(np.array(c_emb))
    all_emb_c = np.array(all_emb_c)
    avg_emb_c = np.mean(all_emb_c, axis=0)
    hyde_vector = avg_emb_c.reshape((1, len(avg_emb_c)))
    return hyde_vector

scenes.caption: The official code puts the query first, then the hypothetical documents. Here N = 3 toy passages from the next lesson.
Each hypothetical passage goes through the same encoder that embedded the corpus.
After the loop the stack is 4 vectors of 4 numbers: query, H1, H2, H3.
Element-wise mean over the 4 rows. This is the HyDE query vector; note its length is about 0.91, not 1.
Reshaped to 1 x d and handed to the searcher, which runs inner product search over the corpus index.

blocks.md: In the released code, the generator samples `n=8` passages with `max_tokens=512`, `temperature=0.7` and stop sequence of three newlines, and the DL19 notebook averages the 8 passages plus the query. The paper used `text-davinci-003`, a GPT-3 instruct-series model, and ran retrieval with the Pyserini toolkit.

Common misconception: HyDE shows the user the generated passage. It does not. The hypothetical document only becomes a vector; everything returned is a real document from the corpus. Hallucinations can still hurt, but by moving the vector, not by being displayed.

blocks.question: In HyDE, which component is trained or fine-tuned for the target task?
options: The Contriever encoder is fine-tuned on the generated passages
Nothing: both the LLM and the encoder are used as-is, only the instruction changes per task
The LLM is fine-tuned to write passages for the corpus
A small adapter maps query vectors to document vectors
blocks.explain: The paper states that no model is trained in HyDE. The only supervision anywhere is the instruction tuning the LLM already received. Adapting to SciFact or FiQA means writing a different instruction.

blocks.question: Your corpus index was built with Contriever. A colleague proposes embedding the hypothetical documents with a different, stronger embedding model to save effort. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, any embedding model works with any index
Only latency increases
The LLM must then be retrained
The vector lands in a different embedding space, so inner products with the indexed Contriever vectors are meaningless
blocks.explain: HyDE relies on document-document similarity inside one space. The hypothetical passage must be encoded by the same encoder f that encoded the corpus, otherwise the averaged vector and the index vectors are not comparable.

lessons.title: Worked toy: how averaging fake answers changes the ranking

blocks.md:
Back to the wisdom tooth query. Suppose the LLM samples N = 3 hypothetical passages, in the spirit of the paper's Figure 1:

- H1: It usually takes between 30 minutes and two hours to remove a wisdom tooth...
- H2: Removing a wisdom tooth is usually quick, often 20 to 45 minutes...
- H3: a passage with invented specifics (a named surgeon, three roots, a 45 minute slot) that drifts toward recovery details.

All three are shaped like answers, so their *question* value is near 0.

blocks.title: Query, hypothetical documents, their average, and the corpus

scenes.caption: Hypothetical documents H1 to H3 put most weight on dental and duration, like the real answers D1 and D2, and almost none on question phrasing.
The HyDE vector is the mean of query, H1, H2, H3. The query's question value 0.74 is diluted to 0.20, because it is now one vote out of four.
Compare the mean with D1 and D3. It now points toward the real answer D1 rather than the FAQ D3.

blocks.prompt: H3 on its own ranks D2 (recovery) first, because its invented details lean toward recovery. After averaging H1, H2, H3 and the query, which document is first?
blocks.reveal: D1, with 0.89 against 0.87 for D2. H1 and H2 both rank D1 first, and their errors differ from H3's, so the average lands near what the samples agree on. This is the paper's expectation estimate at work: sampling several documents and averaging reduces the effect of any one sample's invented details.

blocks.title: Toy scores per query vector (inner product)

scenes.caption: Raw query: FAQ D3 first (0.91), the true answer D1 second (0.60).
H1 alone: D1 0.99 first, D3 drops to last at 0.32. One fake answer already fixes the shape mismatch.
H3 alone (hallucinated specifics): D2 1.00 edges out D1 0.99. A single sample's invented details can reorder the top.
HyDE mean of H1, H2, H3 and the query: D1 0.89, D2 0.87, D5 0.82, D4 0.70, D3 0.47. The real answer is first and the FAQ is last.

blocks.md: Notice the mean vector has length about 0.91, and the official code does not renormalize it. That does not matter for ranking: multiplying the query vector by any positive constant multiplies every document's inner product by the same constant, so the order is unchanged. Scaling the toy mean by 2.5 gives scores 2.23, 2.17, 1.17, 1.75, 2.06, the same order.

blocks.tex: \langle c\,\hat v_q, v_d\rangle = c\,\langle \hat v_q, v_d\rangle \quad (c>0) \;\Rightarrow\; \text{same ranking}
blocks.caption: Normalizing the averaged query vector is optional for ranking, though it changes the raw score values you might threshold on.

blocks.md: How many samples are enough? A simple model: each hypothetical embedding equals the ideal relevance direction $u$ (length 1), plus a shared bias $b$ that every sample repeats (for example a misreading of the query), plus independent noise whose total size is $s$ (in squared length). Averaging N samples shrinks the independent noise to $s/N$ but leaves the shared bias untouched.

blocks.caption: Simplified model: bias orthogonal to u, noise isotropic in high dimension. A Monte Carlo check in 400 dimensions matched the formula (0.693 vs 0.692 at N=1, 0.907 vs 0.907 at N=8, with s=1, b=0.3).

blocks.title: Averaging N samples: noise shrinks, shared bias stays

scenes.caption: s = 1, b = 0.3: cosine rises from 0.69 at N=1 to 0.91 at N=8, and can never pass 0.96 however many samples you draw.
Noisier samples (s = 4) need many more draws: N=8 reaches only 0.79 with b = 0.3. Returns diminish like 1/N in the noise term.
A large shared bias (b = 0.8): the ceiling drops to 0.78. If the LLM misreads the query every time, more samples do not help.

blocks.md: Averaging fixes errors that differ from sample to sample. It cannot fix an error every sample shares, such as the LLM misunderstanding an ambiguous or unfamiliar query. That is the root of HyDE's main failure mode in lesson 5.

blocks.question: You normalize the HyDE mean vector to length 1 before searching an inner-product index. What happens to the top-10 results?
options: They stay the same; only the score values change
They change, because longer vectors favor longer documents
They improve, because cosine is always better than inner product
They get worse, because the query contribution is removed
blocks.explain: Dividing the query vector by its positive length scales every document's score by the same factor, so the ordering is identical. Document vectors are untouched, so this is not the same as switching the whole index from inner product to cosine.

blocks.question: In the simple model with s = 1 and b = 0.3, going from N = 8 to N = 16 samples moves the cosine from about 0.91 to about 0.93. What does this suggest?
options: Always use N = 16
Shared bias is the main error, so prompt changes cannot help
Most of the remaining gap is the shared bias, so doubling generation cost buys little
Averaging hurts beyond N = 8
blocks.explain: The ceiling is 1 over the square root of 1.09, about 0.96. Past N = 8 the independent noise is already small, so extra samples cost tokens for a small gain. Reducing the shared bias (a clearer instruction, keeping the query in the average) is the better lever.

lessons.title: What HyDE achieves, and how query2doc differs

blocks.md: The paper compares HyDE with plain Contriever (same encoder, same index; only the query vector differs), with BM25, and, as references, with retrievers fine-tuned on MS MARCO relevance labels: DPR, ANCE and ContrieverFT (the paper calls ContrieverFT an empirical upper bound). TREC DL19 and DL20 are web search query sets over MS MARCO passages, so the fine-tuned models are in-domain there.

blocks.title: TREC DL web search, HyDE paper Table 1

scenes.caption: DL19 nDCG@10. HyDE lifts Contriever from 44.5 to 61.3, past BM25 (50.6) and close to ContrieverFT (62.1), with no labels.
DL19 recall@1k. HyDE has the highest value of all six systems, 88.0, above every fine-tuned model.
DL20 nDCG@10. HyDE 57.9 against 42.1 for Contriever, but here it trails the fine-tuned models (63.2 to 65.3). Recall@1k is similar to ContrieverFT (84.4 vs 85.8).

blocks.title: BEIR low-resource tasks, nDCG@10 (HyDE paper Table 2)

scenes.caption: Plain Contriever. Note TREC-COVID at 27.3, less than half of BM25's 59.5.
BM25 for reference.
HyDE improves Contriever on all six and beats BM25 on all but TREC-COVID, where it trails by 0.2 (59.3 vs 59.5). ContrieverFT is still ahead on FiQA (32.9) and DBPedia (41.3).

blocks.md: **Multilingual.** On Mr.TyDi (MRR@100), HyDE with multilingual mContriever and an instruction asking for a passage in Swahili, Korean, Japanese or Bengali improves mContriever in every language: Swahili 38.3 to 41.7, Korean 22.3 to 30.6, Japanese 19.5 to 30.7, Bengali 35.3 to 41.3. The gap to the fine-tuned mContrieverFT stays visible (Swahili 51.2), and on Bengali HyDE is slightly below BM25 (41.3 vs 41.8). The authors suggest these languages are under-trained in both the encoder and the LLM.

blocks.title: Generator size matters (HyDE paper Table 4, DL19 nDCG@10)

scenes.caption: Every generator helps unsupervised Contriever, and larger ones help more: 48.9, 53.8, 61.3 against 44.5. The two fine-tuned bars fill in next.
With the fine-tuned encoder, HyDE using InstructGPT still adds 5.3 points on DL19 (62.1 to 67.4). The paper reports smaller LMs can slightly hurt a fine-tuned encoder (Flan-T5: 60.2).

blocks.md:
**query2doc** (Wang, Yang and Wei, 2023) uses the same idea, an LLM writes a pseudo-document for the query, but combines it differently:

- It *concatenates text* rather than averaging vectors. For BM25 the query is repeated n = 5 times then joined to the pseudo-document, so the short query is not drowned out. For dense retrievers it is the query, a [SEP] token, then the pseudo-document, and the dense models are fine-tuned on that input.
- It uses few-shot prompting: 4 labeled (query, passage) examples from MS MARCO in the prompt, so it is not label-free in the strict HyDE sense.

On DL19, BM25 + query2doc reaches nDCG@10 66.2, against 51.2 for BM25 and 61.3 for HyDE (query2doc paper Table 1). Its ablation also shows why keeping the query matters: query only 51.2, pseudo-document only 48.7, both together 66.2. Using the generated text alone can be worse than not expanding at all.

Same ingredient, different plumbing. HyDE: vector space, averaging, unsupervised dense encoder, zero-shot instruction. query2doc: text space, concatenation with the query repeated, works with BM25 or fine-tuned dense models, few-shot prompt. Both pay one LLM generation per query.

blocks.question: On TREC DL19, HyDE has lower nDCG@10 than ANCE (61.3 vs 64.5) but higher recall@1k (88.0 vs 75.5). What is the most reasonable reading?
options: HyDE is broken on precision
HyDE finds more of the relevant documents somewhere in the top 1000, while ANCE orders its top 10 better; a reranker on HyDE's candidates could exploit that
Recall@1k is meaningless for web search
ANCE uses more labels, so its recall should be higher
blocks.explain: The paper notes ANCE's better nDCG@10 but lower recall, suggesting bias toward a subset of queries or documents. High recall makes HyDE a good first-stage candidate generator; precision at the top can come from a reranker.

blocks.question: You add query2doc-style expansion to BM25 but send only the generated passage as the query, dropping the original words. Based on the query2doc ablation, what do you expect on DL19?
options: About 66, the full gain
No change from BM25
A large gain, since the passage contains more terms
Roughly 48.7, slightly below plain BM25 at 51.2
blocks.explain: The ablation reports 48.7 with the pseudo-document only, 51.2 with the query only, and 66.2 with both. The query and the generated passage are complementary; the generated text alone loses the user's exact words.

lessons.title: Latency, cost, and when HyDE hurts

blocks.md: HyDE puts an LLM generation in front of every search. Plain dense retrieval is one short embedding plus an index lookup, typically milliseconds. Generation is autoregressive: one token at a time. The query2doc paper reports its LLM call at over 2000 ms per query (hard to measure precisely, it notes), against 16 ms for a plain BM25 index search; the longer expanded query also slowed the index search to 177 ms.

To reason about N, use a stated model (illustrative numbers, not measurements): time to first token 0.4 s, decoding 40 tokens per second per sequence, 150-token passages, 0.03 s to embed N+1 texts in one batch, 0.01 s for the index search. One passage then takes $0.4 + 150/40 = 4.15$ s.

blocks.title: Where the time goes (simplified latency model)

scenes.caption: Plain dense retrieval: embed the query (0.02 s) and search (0.01 s). Total 0.03 s, too thin to see at this scale.
HyDE with N=1: the generation dominates. Total 4.19 s, over 100 times the plain path.
N=3 as three sequential calls: 12.49 s. Each extra sample adds a full generation.
N=3 sampled in parallel (one request with n=3, as the official generator does, or concurrent calls): back to 4.19 s of wall time, but still 3 times the generated tokens.

blocks.title: Latency vs N under the simplified model

scenes.caption: Defaults: sequential N=8 takes 33.24 s, parallel 4.19 s. Output tokens, and so generation cost, grow as N x L either way: 1200 tokens at N=8.
A fast small model (200 tokens/s) shrinks one passage to 1.15 s. Shorter passages and faster decoding are the main latency levers.
The repo's max_tokens=512 at 40 tokens/s: one passage can take up to 13.20 s. Capping length is a real latency control.

blocks.tex: \text{output tokens per query} = N \times L, \qquad \text{cost per 1000 queries} = \frac{N L p}{1000}
blocks.caption: p is the price in USD per million output tokens. With N=8, L=150 and p=2 that is USD 2.40 per 1000 queries before input tokens; N=1 is USD 0.30. Plug in your provider's current price.

blocks.md: Measured numbers point the same way. Wang et al. (2024) ran HyDE with GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct over the supervised LLM-Embedder on DL19: nDCG@10 went from 70.20 to 75.44 with one passage plus the query, and 75.12 with eight passages plus the query, while the reported per-query latency roughly doubled (7.21 to 14.15). Their full RAG pipeline averaged 11.58 s per query with HyDE retrieval against 1.44 s with plain retrieval.

**Failure 1: ambiguous or unfamiliar queries.** The LlamaIndex HyDE example indexes one Paul Graham essay and asks `What is Bel?`. Without HyDE the answer is right: Bel is a Lisp Graham wrote. With HyDE (one passage plus the original query, the default) the LLM writes about Bel, an ancient Semitic god, and retrieval returns unrelated chunks. Every sample shares that misreading, so averaging cannot remove it.

blocks.title: Toy: the Bel query (programming vs mythology)
labels: C1 Bel, a Lisp in Arc

scenes.caption: Raw query: the right chunk C1 wins with 0.84; the query vector leans on the name Bel and programming.
Hypothetical passage about a mythological god: it matches the culture/art chunk C3 (0.95), not C1 (0.20).
Mean of passage and query, as LlamaIndex does by default: C3 0.58 still beats C1 0.52. Keeping the query halves the damage but does not undo it.

blocks.title: How much weight must the raw query get?

x.label: query weight w in the average

curves.label: wisdom tooth toy: D1 minus D3

scenes.caption: Equal weights give the query w = 1/(N+1). In the wisdom tooth toy HyDE helps for any w below 0.68; in the Bel toy the right chunk needs w above 0.54. More samples lower w and make the Bel case worse.

blocks.md: **Failure 2: biased open-ended queries.** The same LlamaIndex page shows `What would the author say about art vs. engineering?` drifting toward the stance the hypothetical passage took. Abe et al. (2025) study LLM query expansion generally (including query2doc-style answer generation) and find it can significantly degrade retrieval when the LLM lacks knowledge of the query, and that recall gains shrink for highly ambiguous queries.

**Failure 3: strong retrievers.** Weller et al. (2023) tested 11 expansion methods across 24 retrievers and 12 datasets and found a strong negative correlation between a retriever's base score and its gain from expansion. Their setting reranks BM25's top 100 with the generated text added to the query (gpt-3.5-turbo), not HyDE's vector averaging, but the lesson transfers: extra generated text adds noise that blurs the top ranks.

blocks.title: HyDE-style expansion vs retriever strength (Weller et al. Tables 3, 4)

scenes.caption: TREC DL19 nDCG@10: weak DPR gains 18.8 (38.4 to 57.2), ContrieverFT gains 9.3, the strong MonoT5-3B reranker loses 4.0 (71.7 to 67.7).
FiQA (finance, domain shift): DPR +3.6, ContrieverFT -0.3, MonoT5-3B -14.7 (45.9 to 31.2).

blocks.md: **In frameworks.** LlamaIndex's `HyDEQueryTransform(include_original=True)` generates one passage (a code comment marks multiple passages as a TODO), keeps the original query string, and the retriever averages their embeddings with `mean_agg`. LangChain's `HypotheticalDocumentEmbedder.from_llm(llm, base_embeddings, prompt_key="web_search")` ships the paper's prompts, embeds the generated text with `embed_documents` and averages; it does not add the query embedding, so add it yourself if you want equation 8.

Use HyDE where its strength is real: no labels, a weak or unsupervised encoder, domain or format shift, and a latency budget of seconds. Keep the query in the average, cap passage length, sample in parallel, and route by query type. The paper itself suggests serving HyDE early, then shifting traffic to a supervised retriever as logs grow, keeping HyDE for rare and emerging queries.

blocks.question: A support search box must answer in 300 ms at p99. Which HyDE plan is realistic?
options: HyDE with N=8 sequential calls
HyDE with N=8 parallel samples
Do not run HyDE on the request path; use it offline or only for a slow fallback path, and serve plain or hybrid retrieval online
Keep HyDE but drop the embedding step
blocks.explain: Even one generation is seconds in the measurements cited (over 2000 ms in query2doc, 11.58 s per query in the RAG study). Parallel sampling bounds wall time to one generation, which still breaks 300 ms. HyDE fits batch or asynchronous paths, not this budget.

blocks.question: Users of an internal tool type short product code names that the LLM has never seen. HyDE with N=8 is underperforming plain dense retrieval. What is the best first change?
options: Give the raw query far more weight, or skip HyDE for these queries: every sample shares the same misreading, so averaging cannot fix it
Raise N to 32 so the noise averages out
Raise the temperature for more diverse passages
Switch the encoder for the hypothetical passages only
blocks.explain: Unfamiliar names produce a shared bias, which more samples cannot remove (lesson 3), and N=8 even shrinks the query's weight to 1/9. Routing these queries to plain or lexical retrieval, or weighting the query up, addresses the cause. Switching encoders breaks the shared embedding space.

blocks.question: Your stack already uses a strong cross-encoder reranker that scores 72 nDCG@10 on your eval. A teammate wants to add generated passages to the reranker's query. Based on Weller et al., what should you expect and do?
options: A guaranteed gain, as on DPR
Likely no gain or a loss; measure on your own eval before shipping, and consider expansions only for the first stage or for shifted domains
No effect either way
A gain only if N is at least 8
blocks.explain: Weller et al. found strong models are generally harmed: MonoT5-3B lost 4.0 on DL19 and 14.7 on FiQA. Expansion tends to help weaker models or large format shifts, so it must be evaluated, not assumed.
